newsitem.title: SUDAN: FEATURE-Sudan tackles "silent issue" of female circumcision.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Sudan tackles "silent issue" of female circumcision.

text.p: When Awatif Mustafa recalls the day she was circumcised as a seven-year-old, it is her sister's pain and not her own that she remembers most vividly.

"We were two of us. But I remember very clearly it was very difficult for my sister. I could bear it because I was older. But for her she was a bit shy. I can still remember how she shouted," said Mustafa, a 50-year-old university administrator.

"It was kind of a normal thing because of peer pressure. It was a matter of fact," she said of the procedure that involved cutting off the clitoris. "Of course my views have changed. I have two girls of my own and they are not circumcised.
"Because after I got married I had difficulty. Sexual arousal is difficult and it is frustrating for the man. But I was frank about it, I didn't try to hide it."

About 80 percent of women in Sudan are circumcised -- one of the highest rates in Africa -- for cultural and religious reasons. Although the practice also known as female genital mutilation is illegal, social pressures keep it alive.

"It is Sudan's silent issue," said Amna Abdelrahman of the non-governmental Sudan National Committee on Harmful Traditional Practices (SNCTP). "We find our mothers did it and we don't want to abandon links with festivals. Families are used to it."
MOVES TO STAMP OUT PRACTICE

But the Sudan government is working with aid agencies to introduce for the first time a school curriculum focusing on the harmful health and psychological effects of female circumcision, which can lead to sexual dysfunction, infections, inability to pass urine or control it and menstrual problems.

"I think it means they (the government) are strongly recognising this is a problem and it is related to women's rights," said Hanan Suleiman, a UNICEF assistant programme coordinator working with the government on the programme.
And the SNCTP, in an awareness campaign to end the practice, is showing graphic films to social leaders and teaching midwives to make soap as an alternative to circumcision income.

"We started in areas where it is widely spread. We showed community and religious leaders this shocking film," Abdelrahman said of a film showing a screaming two-year-old girl being held down while she is circumcised.
"They said to us they didn't think the operation was like this. We find that midwives continue the practice and try to convince parents because it's a source of income," she said.
AN AGE-OLD RITUAL

Female circumcision has been practised for thousands of years, says anthropologist Hamed al-Bashir. The most severe form is called Pharaonic, which involves cutting off the labia and clitoris and sewing the vagina closed. In Sunna circumcision the clitoris is removed.
"Pharaonic circumcision allows only the penetration of something the size of a matchstick," Bashir said.
"Then after giving birth a woman has to be recircumcised again. It's an endless cycle," Abdelrahman said.
Bashir and Abdelrahman said it is practised because of perceptions that it ensures a woman's chastity, a belief that it is recommended in Islam and to continue cultural traditions.
Abdelrahman said it is performed on girls between ages of two to eight. "But in parts of the east we found girls circumcised who are seven-days-old."
But some women choose to do it for their own reasons.

In a 1995 survey, Bashir said he found old women undergo "circumcision of the grave, when she doesn't want to have any sexual relations. She just wants to hold her beads and meet Allah in a way as if she is just six years old again."
"And a circumcised girl can have a serious sexual relationship before marriage. She can go to the midwife to do restitching. She appears to her husband as if she's a virgin," he said.
"There are also politics involved related to the empowerment of women. For the honeymoon, if a woman is strongly circumcised it might take three weeks to a month for full penetration."

"When a husband can't achieve full penetration he is blackmailed, and he has to pay ransom. For an illiterate woman with no source of income this is the best way for her to get economic power," Bashir said.
EDUCATION MAY BE KEY
Aid agencies say they believe that educating people on the negative effects of female circumcision is one way to eradicate the practice.
SNCTP, UNICEF and Sudan's ministries of health and education are working on a curriculum on harmful traditional practices.
Hanan Suleiman from UNICEF said it would most likely take the form of textbook supplements and a teacher training for the primary levels.
Bashir suggested education was only part of the solution.

"There are some frustrating cases where university women are insisting on the practice because they think it's good for chastity," he said. "If we really want to eradicate this problem we've got to empower women. This is the agony of our culture."
